scenarios.title: Reset behind the blue line in a timing drill
scenarios.objective: Use a named line and an explicit practice condition to coordinate a restart.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. This simplified timing drill has its own instruction: before the coach releases F1 to continue, YOU must return to the neutral-zone side of the right blue line. YOU are currently beyond that line. F1 waits with the puck. This is a practice reset condition, not a complete offside lesson or an officiating ruling.
cues: The coach requires YOU to reset to the neutral-zone side of the right blue line.
The right blue line separates the neutral zone from the attacking end.
F1 is waiting with the puck on the neutral-zone side.

questions.prompt: Where is YOU in relation to the right blue line at this freeze?

options.text: On the right attacking-zone side of the line
At the centre red line
On the neutral-zone side of the right blue line

questions.explanation: YOU are beyond the right blue line in the attacking end. The specified practice reset asks YOU to return to the neutral-zone side.

questions.prompt: Which facts determine whether this stated practice reset is ready?

options.text: YOU’s location relative to the right blue line
The coach’s release instruction
Whether YOU expect F1 to skate quickly later

questions.explanation: The drill explicitly requires a location reset before the coach releases F1. Predicting F1’s later speed does not satisfy those stated conditions.

questions.prompt: Arrange the reset steps given for this timing drill.

options.text: Return to the neutral-zone side of the right blue line.
Check that the coach has released the next action.
Continue the new support route while watching F1 and pressure.

questions.explanation: This sequence follows this exercise’s stated reset. It is not a substitute for learning the applicable full offside rule and its details.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example neutral-zone reset position behind the right blue line for this drill.
questions.explanation: The reference is on the neutral-zone side and gives YOU space separate from F1 and F2. It is an illustrative practice reset, not a geometric offside verdict about a skater’s feet.

questions.prompt: If F1 keeps waiting after YOU reset, what is the useful next check?

options.text: Cross early because F1 will probably move soon.
Check the coach’s release and time your next route with the puck.
Assume the practice condition has disappeared.

questions.explanation: The briefing makes the coach’s release part of this reset. Waiting or moving within the allowed space can be useful while YOU keep F1 and pressure in view.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between following this practice reset and making a full offside call.
questions.explanation: This exercise gives one location-and-release condition. A full rules decision needs the applicable rulebook and details such as the puck, skates and play context, which this simplified freeze does not establish.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate during the reset?

options.text: Reset is the drill instruction; I will check F1 before restarting
The still frame proves offside
The pass must happen now

questions.explanation: The call keeps the practice instruction separate from a formal ruling and adds a restart check.

questions.prompt: Which two cues can delay the restart?

options.text: The coach has not restarted the rep
F1's route or support has changed
The blue line is painted

questions.explanation: The stated restart and current player relationships determine readiness; paint alone does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a different neutral-zone support lane near the right blue line with F1 visible.
questions.explanation: This point is a distinct neutral-zone-side support lane from q4 while keeping F1 visible; it is illustrative and does not establish a formal offside ruling.

questions.prompt: What cue tells you this practice reset is ready to resume?
questions.explanation: Wait for the coach's restart and re-check F1's route. The position alone does not establish a formal rule call or timing.

scenarios.title: Update the play when the coach stops the rep
scenarios.objective: Recognize that a stated stop signal changes a loose-puck race into a controlled reset.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU and gold D1 had been approaching a loose puck in the neutral zone. The coach has just whistled and clearly called “stop this rep.” This is an explicit practice instruction. No official penalty or game stoppage is being inferred.
cues: The coach explicitly stopped this practice rep.
Other skaters remain near the approach routes.

questions.prompt: What has changed the task even though the puck remains loose?

options.text: Gold D1 has confirmed possession of the loose puck
The original race is still the active task
The coach has explicitly stopped this rep.

questions.explanation: The briefing gives the coach’s whistle and clear stop instruction. The puck is still unowned, but the current practice task is no longer to win the race.

questions.prompt: Which actions fit the stopped-rep instruction?

options.text: Stop competing for the puck and control your movement
Keep awareness of nearby skaters as you reset
Make one more challenge before listening

questions.explanation: The stopped rep calls for a controlled reset with awareness of others. A final challenge would continue the contest the coach has just ended. Technique and stopping room need on-ice instruction.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested response to the clear stop call.

options.text: Recognize the rep has ended.
Control movement while checking nearby skaters.
Listen for the next setup or coaching cue.

questions.explanation: The routine connects the signal to a controlled reset. It does not specify a braking technique or a distance every player can safely use.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example open reset location away from the loose-puck contest. Describe how you would get there under control.
questions.explanation: The reference separates YOU from the puck and D1’s current area. It is a reset destination for discussion, not proof of a safe immediate stopping path; actual speed, skill and other skaters matter.

questions.prompt: If the coach then restarts with F2 as the puck carrier, what should YOU confirm before beginning again?

options.text: Your new support role and the new puck situation
That the old loose-puck race still applies
That the old approach route is still open

questions.explanation: A new setup can give YOU a new responsibility. Confirm the coach’s instruction and current possession rather than carrying over the previous race.

questions.prompt: Why can the right decision change even when no player has touched the puck?
questions.explanation: The coach’s explicit instruction changed the task. Game information includes stated signals and constraints as well as puck location; here the useful response is a controlled reset and attention to the next instruction.

questions.prompt: What should YOU acknowledge when the coach stops the rep?

options.text: The contest is paused and I will reset under control
The puck is still fair to battle
F2 owns it now

questions.explanation: The stop call changes the task even though the puck is loose.

questions.prompt: Which two checks belong at the restart?

options.text: Who the coach assigns as carrier
Where D1 and F2 are now
The old loose-puck plan

questions.explanation: Restart assignment and current player positions define the new read.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a reset space clear of the loose-puck contest.
questions.explanation: This point separates YOU from the contest and leaves room to hear the restart.

questions.prompt: F2 is assigned the puck at restart. Explain how the first support decision changes.
questions.explanation: Confirm F2's location and D1's pressure, then choose a support angle based on the new carrier rather than the stopped rep.

scenarios.title: Show a safe wall-side escape
scenarios.objective: Scan the pressure and make a reachable first exit after a wall pickup.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks +x. YOU approaches a loose puck beside the left wall; D1 is above you and F2 is inside the ice. The rep asks for the first exit after control, not a certain pass.
cues: The puck is loose at the wall.
D1 is above the puck; F2 is a middle outlet.
The first exit must be re-read after control.

questions.prompt: Which two details belong in your first escape read?

options.text: D1's approach side
F2's reachable support angle
A promise that the middle pass will be open

questions.explanation: Pressure and support describe why an escape could work; if either changes, keep the puck protected and reconsider.

questions.prompt: Arrange a careful wall-pickup plan.

options.text: Check D1 and F2
Control the loose puck
Choose the exit that remains reachable

questions.explanation: Look at the named pressure and outlet, control the puck, then use the updated lane; the order does not guarantee the pass.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an approach point just inside the wall that keeps F2 visible.

questions.prompt: D1 drops toward F2 before your touch. What should change first?

options.text: Protect the puck and scan a different exit
Pass inside immediately because F2 was the first outlet
Carry toward F2 through the middle even though D1 has dropped into that lane

questions.explanation: D1 closing the middle changes the named outlet; protecting the puck buys a chance to find a wall-side or return option.

questions.prompt: If F2 is still visible but D1 closes the middle, explain how you would communicate and re-read the escape.
questions.explanation: Name that D1 has taken away the middle lane, communicate that the outlet is conditional, and say what wall-side or return space you would check before choosing a touch.

scenarios.title: Receive on the far shoulder
scenarios.objective: Receive away from pressure while keeping both the passer and next option available.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks +x. F1 carries near the left hash marks and is preparing a pass; YOU is open to the right, with D1 between the intended lane and the boards. F2 is farther up ice.
cues: D1 is closer to the inside of YOU than F1 is.
F2 is a possible next option, not a promised pass.

Whether F1 can reach the new spot cleanly

questions.prompt: Arrange this receiving decision.

options.text: Scan behind and inside
Present a reachable target to F1
Receive under control and choose the next option

questions.explanation: The scan informs the target, then the touch can be adjusted to the pressure and the available continuation.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a receiving point with more separation from D1 and a visible lane from F1.

options.text: Open your body to protect the puck and keep a return option
Turn fully up ice before the puck arrives
Demand the same forward turn even if the lane is covered

questions.explanation: D1 has removed the easy inside turn, so a protected touch and a conditional return preserve more choices.

questions.prompt: Why can a wider receiving angle help here, and what would make you change it?
questions.explanation: A wider angle can separate YOU from D1 while preserving F1's lane. Change it if D1 follows or F1 loses a clean route, then re-offer a reachable option.

scenarios.title: Re-offer after the first lane is covered
scenarios.objective: Change the support relationship when a defender stays in the original passing line.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks +x. F1 has the puck near the middle; YOU is to the right, but D1 occupies the direct line. F2 is wide and can become useful if D1 follows the re-offer.
cues: D1 sits between F1 and YOU.
F2 is wide on the far side.
A new angle may change which teammate becomes available.
